On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Volunteer Bounty Act, and its amending

Acts, by providing that the time within which any grantee or his duly qualified substitute may surrender to the Crown all rights under the said Volunteer Bounty Act, 1908, and may thereupon be paid the sum of five hundred dollars out of such moneys as are voted for that purpose by Parliament, to be extended to the 31st December, 1914.
This does not affect the Volunteer Bounty Act which was passed about two years ago in connection with the Department of Militia?
It has nothing to do with that.

As the Minister of Militia is not in his seat, can the hon. minister give any information as to whether legislation will be introductd to provide for an extension of time with regard to the other bounty Act?	'	.
Yes.
How many certificates are outstanding?
Forty-eigh*
How many persons have taken advantage of the legislation of a year ago?

I have not the figures before me, but I may say that there was a provision in last year's Bill whereby those who did not file upon their land by October 31, 1913, would, by surrendering their certificates to the department, receive the sum of $500. It appears that quite a number of persons were not aware of the fact that in order to obtain this amount it was necessary that they should surrender their certificates before that date, and it is in order to extend the time within which they may surrender their certificates that this resolution is introduced.
I think we should have information as to how many persons took advantage of the opportunity afforded them a year ago for taking a cash surrender.
I think 'comparatively few have done so. As I have said, forty-eight certificates are still outstanding. I will obtain the information and give it to my hon. friend on the second reading of the Bill.

Will the minister not
make a finality of this matter in the proposed legislation? The matter has been before Parliament at least four times, possibly more.

It seems to me to be worse than unfair to extend this repeatedly. Every time this matter comes up in Parliament-and I think I can blame the former minister as much as the present minister-we have been promised that this would be the end, that there would be no more extensions of time; and yet, every year, there is a further extension, not for the benefit of the volunteer, but really for that of the speculator. I venture to say that out of the forty-eight there are not four that are in the hands of the men who earned them; they are practically all in the hands of specu lators. Why should this Parliament year after year pass legislation simply to protect a few men who have gambled in land and lost. It is putting a premium on gambling.

I think the hon. member
is confused between the two cases. This is not an extension of time to file on their lands; this is an extension of the time within which they can present their certificates and get the cash grant of $500. The hon. member is in error in saying that there have been repeated extensions for the purpose of this resolution. Last year was the first extension of this kind. There has been quite a number of extensions for the time of filing, but last year an extension was granted largely on the representations of the hon. member for Edmonton, who pointed out some hardships on certain men by reason of the preceding extensions, which he thought should be given consideration. The matter was considered during my absence, although I introduced the amendment to the Bill, but I purposely made it the 31st of October so that there would be no misunderstanding in the country. A pledge was given in the House during the last session that no further extension would be granted for filing on the land. That has been lived up to; but last year was the first year in which a cash appropriation was made by which those who did not file on the land could secure the $500. I am extending the time because I thought it was a hardship, that a good many of those who held the grants were not aware that the extension of time to surrerfder their certificates had expired at the same time as the extension to file upon the land, so I am merely providing an extension of the time at which they can surrender the certificates and get the $500. The information asked for I can furnish on the second reading of the Bill.

I quite appreciate the
distinction my hon. friend draws, and there is some reason in it. On the other hand, my hon. friend must confess that while he has carried out the pledge made by the Minister of Public Works -that there would be no further extension of the time literally, he has not carried it out practically. My hon. friend has been in public life long enough to know that you cannot devise a condition of affairs in which some interested party will not come here and represent that he has been misled and apply for a change of the law. Undoubtedly they can make more money by holding off -and asking the minister to exend the time.
How can they make more money?

They will in some way come back and say -that they have held the land a long time iand they think they should get, instead of $500, $700 or $800. I do not say the minister will grant it but they will ask for it. In ,my own province there were hundreds of these volunteers; in my own town I think we had forty or fifty. We are innocent people down east and we believe the substance of the law and many volunteers sold out their scrip for $150 or $160, because they believed what Parliament said. Some got $400 or $500 and some who were not so innocent got as high as $800 or $900. However, they were all sold and bought by -speculators, most of whom are in the city of Winnipeg. Now the speculator has found that he has gambled an<J lost and Parliament. intervenes in order to protect him against an unsound business proposition. He should pocket his loss as any of the rest of us do when we make an unprofitable business -speculation. I do not suppose my protest will defeat the Bill but if I had power to defeat it I would do so.
Mr. RO-OHE: If we were asking an extension of th-e time in which these warrants might be filed on the land the hon. gentleman's argument would be quite appropriate but it is not appropriate to the present amendment of the Act which I propose to introduce. It is impossible for men to make more money by delaying and it is not the intention to amend the Act to increase the amount to more than $500. Five hundred it is, -and no matter how long they may hold it they cannot make another dollar out of it because they cannot -speculate with it. *1 have never given my pledge in the House about it, but this is the only



time an extension has been granted for the $500 and it is the only time there will be such an extension. If they do not see fit to surrender their certificates by the 31st of December, 1914, they will have to go without their money. The best evidence that the holders of these certificates did not surrender them because they were unaware of this provision of the Act is that they had nothing to gain by holding.

And you had the
use of the money in the meantime.
And we had the use of the money in the meantime.	'
They will expect interest upon that.
They will make application but their application will receive no consideration other than is provided for >y last year's Act.
Has the minister any information in his department by which be can tell who are the holders of the scrip?
We have not the names of the holders but we can tell as to whether they are the original holders or not.
Would it not be advisable to send notice to these people that this will be the last extension in order that their rights might be protected?
We could do so.

I would like to ask
the minister if it would not be possible to restrict the advantage of the renewals to the original holders of the certificates. There may be some equities in their case but I think there are no equities in the case of the speculators who held these certificates previously to the 31st October. To my mind there is a very great distinction between the equities of the one and the claims of the other. One has equities, the other has claims. The position taken by the minister is a reasonable one if we apply his argument in favour of the original holders, the one who earned the grant, the one to whom the certifi 'ate was granted and to whom ad the advantages of it should apply.
Right Hon. Sir WILFRID LAHRIER [DOT] My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) is very technical when he says that this is the first instance of a renewal for a grant of money. There have been renewals once or twice under this Act but these renewals were not to get a money grant, but to allow the holders of the certificates fur-

ther time to file their claims. They were allow one renewal and then another. This is a renewal to allow them to make an application for a grant of money which they had earned by their failure to apply for the land. But this distinction is a very technical one after all. We have amended the Act once, twice and three times over. I do not say that the legislation this year may not be justified by the circumstances, a knowledge of which may be in the possession of the minister. Last year,- at the time of the last renewal, I think a sufficient reason was given why the Act should be renewed but it was understood that it would be the last time. There must be some finality to this matter. My hon. friend asks for this legislation; it is exceptional legislation and legislation which is exceptional in its character ought to be supported by good and sufficient reasons. The only reproach I have to make to my hon. friend's that he has not fortified himself with sufficient reasons if we are to judge by those which he has given to the House. I do not intend to oppose the resolution at this stage but before the matter comes up again for discussion on the second reading of the Bill my hon. friend must lay on the Table of the House all the reasons which he has and which, in his opinion, are sufficient to justify such legislation so that every member of the House may be in a position to judge whether or not there ought to be another extension of time.

I would like to ask the minister what he does in connection with persons who have entered upon the land, who, of course, have covenanted to perform the homestead duties and against whom there is an application for cancellation. What does the minister do with these people? Does he cancel them off the face of the earth or give them credit for what they have done?
What is that?

We will suppose that A paid a thousand dollars to buy a South African warrant, he has entered on the land and through unforeseen circumstances he has.not been able to perform the homestead duties and the entry is cancelled; what does the minister do with that man? Does that man get any compensation or is he out his thousand dollars?

He is out his thousand
dollars.

When a volunteer or his substitute has entered for a specific piece

of land, does the minister ever permit the entrant to change his land?
I have no knowledge of any instance of the kind having taken place. I do not think there has been any application of that kind before me. I have no recollection of such a case.

Will the minister be
kind enough to get information on that point because I remember it was a very important, and quite a difficult, point When the former Government were in power? Men sometimes made a mistake, or were misinformed, about the land, it was not worth what they paid for the scrip and consequently they did not perform any of the duties. I would like to know what the practice of the department is in that and other cases.

I would like very much to have heard the reasons that the minister has in mind for proposing his legislation. I would like to have known at whose instance the minister has introduced it. Is it for the sake of the original holders of the scrip or for the sake of the substitutes who purchased this scrip for speculative purposes? That is the information that I think the committee is fairly entitled to before the minister should ask us to agree to this resolution. It seems to me that we are never going to get to the end of this South African veteran's scrip proposition. Year after year we have granted extensions and now we are confronted with the question of an extension of time for the payment of this $500 to the holders of the scrip. What reasons have the substitutes who hold the scrip given to the minister Why they did not take advantage of the provision by which they might surrender the scrip last year for $500? Why did they not do it? If the holders of the scrip failed to take advan-take of that provision why is Parliament asked this year to extend the time for the presentation of the scrip?

I have already given all the information, but I have no objection to giving the reasons over again. In the first place, it was brought to my attention by the officers of my department that they were in receipt of a number of letters from the holders of these warrants, some of whom had sent down their certificates since the 31st of October, 1913, and had asked for the $500. The officers of the department had to write to these persons telling them that their' warrants were of no use now because they had not sur-894
rendered them to the department within the time specified by the Act of last year. This was owing to the fact that the holders were not aware that the extension covered the surrendering of their certificates; they thought it applied only to filing on the lands. They did not know that it was necessary to send their certificates in and register them in the department within that date. It is because of their request for the payment of the $500 grant since the 31st October, that my officials think there should be an amendment covering that part of the Act.
I understand that the minister has stated that forty-eight scrips will be affected. How many of these scrips are in the hands of the original holders and how many in the hands of assignees ?

That question has been asked me on two occasions, and I said that I would be able to give the House all the information on the second reading of the Bill. I do not remember how many of the forty-eight certificates are in the hands of the original owners, but I presume there are not very many.
I would like to ask the minister if this extension only applies to the holders of certificates who hold them at the expiration-of the former Act?
Yes.
In case of the transfer of one of these warrants after the 31st of October, 1913, this legislation would not apply ?
No.

This legislation is very closely akin to another volunteer bounty matter, and I beg your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, for bringing to the notice of the minister the situation in respect to the Act which was passed in 1912 with reference to the Fenian Eaid bounty. The Act of the 1st of April, 1912, expired on the last day of 1913, and about 16,000 applications were then in. Some of these were passed upon by the department and some are being held for consideration, and I understand there is no authority to deal with them one way or the other. We aTe receiving a great many inquiries as to when the Government will be able to deal with these applications, which have not yet been passed upon. I understand that 14,000 applicants have been paid, and those who have not been paid and who stood in the same ranks with the others, are sensitive

about the matter and feel that they have been discriminated against. I wish to know when the Government purposes taking power to finally deal with this subject and wind it up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that the
Minister of Militia has already stated to the House that legislation will be introduced this session. I shall draw the attention of the minister to the observations of my hon. friend.

My recollection is that
these warrants were issued to the volunteers, and there was a provision in the law that they were not assignable more than once. In order to get around that, the volunteer assigned in blank, and the holder simply fills in his name when the warrant is brought to the department. Has the minister information as to who are the actual present holders of these forty-eight warrants?
The department would have information as to how many are in the hands of the original owners, tout the department has no information as to those others who hold the warrants at the present time.

These warrants might
pass through a dozen different hands and the minister would only know the name of the person who surrenders the warrant to the department.

I do not know anything
about the number of hands they would pass through, but whatever information there is in the department I shall bring down.

Last year the Minister of the Interior was not able to take charge of the Bill, for reasons which we all regretted, and it was in the hands of the Minister of Labour, who was acting Minister of the Interior. When the Bill came before the House, I urged that if the scrip were worth $500 up to the 31st of October, it should be worth that amount after the 31st of October, and I asked the acting minister that he should name a day, subsequent to the date on which the scrip might be located, for the redemption in money. The acting minister said that the 31st of October was the last day for the redemption in money, and he would not consider the suggestion I made, but which evidently has impressed itself upon the mind of the minister (Mr. Roche): that there should be extension of time given for the payment of the money. What reasons

have impressed themselves upon the present minister, to have additional legislation this year, which did not occur to tne acting minister last year?

Excise-Salaries of officers and inspectors of excise, and to provide for increase depending on the result of excise examinations, $565,278.75.
['Yes.\nBill reported, read the third time and passed.']

I did not want to
bother the minister when this item was under consideration last night, but there are some things I would like to know now. Are these promotion examinations conducted under the Civil Service Commission; who sets the questions and passes upon the papers?
The result of the examination before the Civil Service Commission is brought before a board composed of the superior officers of the department, Mr. Lawlor, Mr. Gow, and other inspectors.

Are those questions
printed and are they available to the public, so that they can see the nature of the questions? Taking any special case, I would like to know the nature of the paper set for a candidate for promotion.
The questions relate to the excise and manufactures. They are not submitted to the public, but are handed to the applicants at the examination.
Are they written examinations?
Yes.
They are not competitive examinations?

The examinations for
special-class excisemen are competitive.
This item is composed of two parts: one part is for increase and the other is for new officers. How much is for new officers and how much for increase?

The increase of $37,471.75 i.3 for deputy collectors-class B. The increase especially for the third-class' officers is $10,975. The new appointments in that class are: A. Boucher, J. A. Oliver, John Fry, F. H. Farnsworth, E. McNally, G. X.
Bainey, J. E. Barrette, J. 0.
4 p.m. Prevosfc, J. Prevost, G. O'Neil, P. E. C. Joubert, Geo. Boux, B. M. Miller. They reach respectively $700 and $800 a year.

After taking off the
amount for the pay of these new officers, what is left to be applied to the increase ?

There is a regular increase by regulation for about thirteen employees, receiving an increase of $100 a year for a portion of a year. Some receive $75 for nine months; others $50 for five or six months, * and the balance $25 for three months.

Is there enough left,
after payment of the fixed charges, for the payment of the new officers?
Yes.
I understand that the minister has made a new appointment at Sydney. C.B. What is his salary?
We have appointed Mr. E.	T. MacKeen, at a salary of $900 a year.
Is Mr. MacKeen receiving that salary this year?
Yes.

What was the salary
of his immediate predecessor?
The same salary.

There is no increase
given to the new officer?
No.
Can the minister give us the number of preventive officers in the province of Quebec?
Temporary officers?

The preventive officers.
I do not believe they are permanent. In the meantime, the minister might perhaps give the committee a synopsis of the work performed by the preventive officers.
The duties of the preventive officers are to prevent the violation of the law regarding liquor, to endeavour to discover illicit stills, and to prevent any violation of the law regarding tobacco.
Do they receive a regular-salary or are they paid when they make a seizure?
The temporary preventive officers are Dr. L. P. Lavallee, G.. S. Warren . . .
Is Dr. L. P. Lavallee Sl physician?

He is a preventive officer and also a food inspector. Some of these, besides being preventive officers, are food inspectors or excise men. Some of them hold positions as assistant inspectors of weights and measures.

Has the hon. minister
any preventive officer in the district of Beauce?

Here is a list of preventive officers who, though at the head office at Quebec, work in the .surrounding counties of Quebec:	G. S. Warren, L. P.
Lavallee, G. Bouliane, P. Courey, P. E. Menard, A. Pelletier, W. LeBel, J. Dupont,
F.	X. Boy. All these belong to the district of Quebec.

There was a preventive
officer named Lambert at Beauceville. Is he still employed in the department?
He was dismissed.
Has the minister a preventive officer at Swift Current? Or was the officer there dismissed, and, if so, why?

There is no preventive
officer at Swift Current.

I have not given the
title of the position correctly, then. There is a representative of the department at Swift Current I know.

Can you give me his
name?

Mr. Edmanson was
there when the Liberals were in power, but I think he was dismissed.

Yes, he was dismissed
and not replaced.
Why was he dismissed, and when?
I will have the list looked over.
Does the preventive officer receive a portion of the proceeds of sale made in consequence of seizure?
The officer receives half the penalty after all expenses are paid.
What does the minister mean by ' after all expenses are paid' ? Generally, when a man is found guilty on an action brought against him, costs go with the action.
If there are no expenses, of course, there is no deduction. But there are travelling and other expenses, and it seems to me that they should be paid.
Am I to understand that the travelling expenses of preventive officers are paid out of the seizures made?
Preventive officers receive a fixed amount of salary, and besides they are entitled to receive a part of the amount of seizures. *

I understand that. But Is it not true that an allowance is made them for travelling expenses? If an officer goes through, let us say, the province of Quebec, and makes no seizures, who pays his travelling expenses?
When they are sent out especially and incur expenses, they are paid their expenses besides their salary.

Then, the expenses of the preventive officer travelling for the department are paid by the department, and when a preventive officer makes a seizure, half the fine is so much added to his salary and travelling expenses? The minister says,
' yes.'
. Mr. BELAND:	What amount was received last year for seizures?
About $2,800.
Mr. Frenette still holds the same position but he is to be transferred to Quebec. He now belongs to the head office at Quebec.
Must I understand that the position of excise officer at Fraserville is abolished, and that it is decided that this man will be transferred to Quebec?

Yes.
[ Mr. Nantel.]
Will his salary be increased ?
For the present, his salary is the same as the one he had at Fraserville.
What is the salary?
$900 a year.

Does the minister suppose that a man can live on a salary of $900 in a city like Quebec ? Is it the intention of the minister to increase the salary of Mr. Frenette, if there is something left of this vote of $13,000 ?
Mr. Frenette's salary is exactly $850. Being transferred to Quebec, he will necessarily receive more.
Can I take the word of the minister for that ?
Certainly.

I am not concerned with the case of Mr. Frenette because he is a political friend of mine; on the contrary, he has always been opposed to me politically; but I do not ask for the sinner's death and I want the minister to give him a salary he can live upon.
His salary will be increased.

Last night, I did not mention the dismissals that have taken place in my county, for the reason that the one I had in mind concerned a preventive officer. Mr. Elie Martin, preventive officer of St. Arsene, has been dismissed. I would like to know if the minister has received a petition or solemn declaration-I understand that declarations under oath must not be mentioned-charging Mr. Martin of political partisanship. The minister, it seems to me, is not ready to answer. I did not suppose that my question would occasion such a loss of time. That is the trouble of having a minister that is never ready to answer the questions put by members, and who has not at hand the information asked for.

Mr. Martin was a temporary preventive officer at Quebec, with a salary of $300. His services were not required. There has been no investigation held. There has been no sworn declaration. Mr. Martin was only a temporary officer and iso he could be dismissed at any time; he had five days' notice.
Then the minister has taken upon himself to cut his head off, without any formality.

Mr. Martin was employed as a temporary preventive officer during the holidays, for an indefinite period; we have many others in the same position.
Mr. GATJVREATJ; Was his dismissal recommended by any one P
I have not here the papers concerning Mr. Martin s case, but I can have them if it is so desired.

I understand that the department had to make room in Temis-couata, to appoint a friend of the Government, and that is why Mr. Martin has been dismissed. Mr. Martin is a man who has been very useful to the department by the intelligent discharge of his duty. His nomination was the first official act of Mr. Bernier, in taking charge of the Department of Inland Revenue. I am not aware that a single complaint has been laid against Mr. Martin, and I am yet asking myself why the minister has dismissed him, since there was no complaint. The only reason the minister can give is that a place had to be found for a political friend.
I cannot give you any more information for the time being.

Was it by means of the Hertzian waves that the minister learned that there was in the county of Temiscouata a Liberal who should be replaced by a friend of his party? At any rate, I think it only fair I should post the House as to the qualifications of the man who has been appointed in place of Mr. Martin.	.
Mr. Nazaire Lebel was appointed in his place; and should we fall from power, you will dismiss us in the same way.
Is the minister aware that at this very time Mr. Nazaire Lebel is one of the political organizers for the county of Temiscouata and that he is constantly interfering in politics.
Not at all. If he meddles with politics, he will be dealt with in the same way as all others, and removed from office.

I believe the minister is too much of a party man to do that, and if he intends keeping his word, he had better put that man out at once, for I am going to prove that he is right in the thick of the political fray. Here is an instance I wish
to quote to give an idea of the man who has been appointed to replace Mr. Martin. Aware of the fight which is being made in the province of Quebec with a view to improving the highways, that same Mr. Lebel takes every opportunity to state all over the constituency, at the church doors, that no heed should be given to the provincial act relating to the improvement of roads, seeing that the Dominion Government has enacted a measure whereby farmers will have good roads without paying a cent for the work.
That is an actual fact.

Is the hon. Postmaster General ready to state on behalf of the Government that the latter will take charge of the highways without exacting a cent from any one? I believe he will not dare to interfere to that extent with the powers of the Minister of Railways. Moreover, I am satisfied neither the Minister of Railways nor the Prime Minister would be willing to bind themselves to that extent.
I may state to the hon. member that whenever the Senate agrees to pass that Bill, the municipalities will not be called upon to pay the interest charges.

I realize that when it comes to winning an electoral contest, hon. gentlemen will be ready to make any kind of promise.
In any case, I may say to the Minister of Inland Revenue that the man he has chosen to replace Mr. Martin is a party heeler who does nothing else from one end of the year to the other. Now, the minister is not obliged to take my word for it; but if he enquires, he will have no difficulty in getting the proof of the facts as set forth by me. Mr. Martin is a man of quiet and peaceful habits, so much so, that I am not at all sure that he votes at elections, and that, of course, would only be exercising his rights as a citizen. I wonder what has put in the minister's head that he must put him out and replace him by a party heeler who will get thereby $300 per annum.
I thought fit, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of the House to that unfair dismissal. I realize that such an act is of no concern to my hon. friend, who is well padlocked and bolted to his portfolio. But if in the future he finds that his men do not meddle quite so much with politics, he may give me some credit for it.

The hon. member for
Moosejaw asked a question with reference to the dismissal of R. W. Edmanson, who

*was temporarily employed 'as an excise officer at Swift Current. His salary was $250, and he was employed also as a customs officer. He was dismissed by the hon. Minister of Customs for political partisanship.
Mr. KNOWLES [DOT] On which side was he forking?
I suppose he was working for the Liberal party.
Is my hon. friend just guessing?
That is the letter I received, I suppose.
Does the file show he was working for the Liberals?
No, it has been decided by the Depart nent of Customs.
Does it say the Liberal side on the file?
Yes. It conveys that idea.

Would the minister
please read us the part in which it says that?
I say he has been dismissed for political partisanship.
It does not say which side?
The Liberal side.

Would the minister
read the part which says Liberal side?

Surely you can make
your own deduction.

I ask the minister, who has used this document in the diseussioji, which I presume we could ask to have laid on the table of the House, to read the part of it which says that he worked on the Liberal side. It is simply political partisanship.
Yes.
Then the minister is only guessing when he says Liberal?
Yes, I am sure of it. I am sure he was working on the Liberal side.
The cat is out of the bag; they would not dismiss a man if it was on the Conservative side he was acting.
Certainly not.

And there we have the confession from the minister that they dismiss Liberals and promote Conservatives who are partisans. The minister says: It does not say on the file that he was a Liberal; but from the fact that he was dismissed for political partisanship I know he must be a Liberal. On whose recommendation was he dismissed?
Hon. J. D. Reid, Minister of Customs.
On whose recommendation did the Minister of Customs Act.

He is not here. This
officer was a temporary officer, and I consider I was justified in dismissing him on the Order in Council passed at the request of the Customs Department. As a matter of fact, he was working for the Inland Revenue Department only on commission.
I understood the minister to say that he got $250.
And $50 provisional allowance.
I understood the minister to say he got $250; now I understand that he received $300.

He receives $250 on a
commission basis and $50 as a provisional allowance, ia total of $300.

Does the minister assert that the fact that another minister of the Crown dismisses an official who happens to be working for his department would be a good cause for dismissal in the Inland Revenue Department without any investigation? I do not think that is fair and I want to know the minister's views.

I would not like to liy
down a general rule.

Suppose the Minister
of Militia had some man employed as caretaker for his department in my hon. friend's county. Suppose the Minister of Militia dismissed that man because he was a Nationalist, would my hon. friend dismiss him because the Minister of Militia dismissed him?

I would consider the
question. The Department of Customs having dismissed him, as he was working on commission from the Department of Inland Revenue he was not entitled to receive the commission because he was deprived of his office in the Customs Department.
Then when the minister told us that he was dismissed for being a partisan that was not a correct answer, the reason is that he was only temporary?

He was dismissed for
political partisanship by the Customs Department, and on the receipt of the minister's letter I dismissed him. I consider I was perfectly justified in acting in that way, because I have no doubt the Minister of Customs was right in his action.

Am I right in assuming
from the answer of the minister that temporary employees in his department can be dismissed without any reason other than the fact that they are temporary employees.

I consider so, and when they are so employed they are frankly notified that they are only temporary officials. In the list of dismissals of yesterday there were several who were officers only during the holidays. They could not expect to remain in the service for years and years.

Take the case of a man like Mr. St. Pierre, in Montreal, who has been an employee of the department for about twenty-one years, and is still a temporary employee because he has not passed any examination. Are we to understand that the minister has laid down a rule that a temporary employee can be dismissed from his department simply because somebody else comes rapping at the door, without any other reason than the fact that he is temporarily employed ? I would ask the minister if he is in a position to-day to tell us how there came to be such a discrepancy between his statement on the floor last night that he had only dismissed eighty-four employees in his department since he was appointed to office and the return which was tabled at the request of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), which shows that one hundred and one employees were dismissed within the first year. The minister told me last night, after the adjournment of the committee, that he would take the matter up with the officers of his department and have an answer for the committee to-day. I would await that answer.

The whole number of officials removed from my department since the 19th of October, 1911, is 102. Of these fifty-five were permanent officers, ten were removed by death, seven were super- * annuated, ten resigned, fifteen were removed for political partisanship, twelve for
intemperance. Among the temporary officers, forty-seven were removed. Of these, thirteen resigned, six were removed for political partisanship, and twenty-eight for intemperance or other causes.
What has become of the nine men who the minister said yesterday were dismissed because their services were no longer required ?

These nine men were: Louis 0. Belliveau, Montreal; James Lynch, Montreal; J. W. Bohan, St. John; Louis Basinet, Joliette; Dr. 0. E. Milot, Three Rivers; J. B. St. Pierre, Montreal; E. Richer, St. Hyacinthe; William MacBeth, Montreal; Archibald MacDonald, Mull river; Elie Martin, Quebec; Odillon Pelletier, Quebec; J. E. Rivet, Joliette; D. Chisholm, Pictou; E. A. Lambert, Beauceville; Ls. M. Trottier, St. Hyacinthe.

I am not questioning the right of the minister to dismiss his employees, but the point I am trying to get at is this: how is it if they were dismissed because, as the minister just now says, their services were no longer required, in the list that he has given I do not find any of the nine names given in the return as having been dismissed on account of their services being no longer required? There are other reasons given in the list; still, in the return brought down to the House the reason given is that their services are no longer required. It seems to me that the return is incorrect.
The return is correct.

Then, the statement of
the minister is incorrect.

I must admit that I had a list yesterday which was incorrect. There were some errors in it. This morning I saw the officers of the department, I went into the list and I ascertained that the return was correct except that it did not contain all the names. I think there were one or two more names.

The minister now admits that the statement he gave the House last evening with reference to the number of dismissed employees was incorrect and I would now ask him if he is prepared to correct the statement that he made yesterday that no employees were dismissed after the 10th December, 1912.

I am perfectly willing
to correct that statement in accordance with the one I have just made.
Who has been appointed as the successor of Mr. John C. Bourinot who was dismissed in my county?

Was he an excise or a
preventive officer?

He was a customs
detective.

We have no such name
in our list; he belongs to the customs.
Last night, when the minister was reading the names of those who had been dismissed, I heard that of Archibald MacDonald, of Mull River. Whom has he appointed as the successor of Mr. MacDonald?
Archibald MacDonald has been succeeded by Archibald G. MacDonald as a temporary preventive officer.
Who recommended the appointment of Archibald G. MacDonald as successor to Archibald MacDonald and the dismissal of the latter?
I am not in a position to give the name of the gentleman who recommended him.
Will the minister furnish me with that information when his Estimates come up again?
Certainly.
Has the minister the name of Angus R. Macdonald who was dismissed about a year and a half ago? He had to look after illicit stills and that sort of thing.
I have no such name. Does he not belong to the customs?
I am not sure; I know that among his duties was looking after illicit stills.
We have no such name.

I would like the minister to give us an explanation of the difference between this item and the next. This item is:
Extra duty-pay at large distilleries and other factories.
Then, the next item is:
Duty-pay to officers serving longer hours at other than special surveys.
What is the difference between extra duty and longer hours?

Longer hours apply to
officers in charge of bonded factories.

What is the meaning of
extra duty pay at large distilleries. Is that for officers working overtime?
For overtime and extra responsibility in connection with the work of important warehouses.
I would like to ask the minister who is now the deputy minister and what changes have taken place in the staff at headquarters during the past year.

The deputy minister is
Mr. Himsworth and the assistant is Mr. Vincent.
When was Mr. Himsworth made deputy minister?
He has been deputy minister since the 1st of October, 1913.
Whom did he succeed?
Mr. Gerald.
When did he retire?

On the 1st of October,
1912.
Who was the assistant deputy minister under Mr. Gerald?
Mr. Himsworth was the secretary and assistant deputy minister.
Was Mr. Vincent in the department before the time of his appointment?
Mr. Vincent was not in the department.

Had he had any
particular training and experience in the work of the department that would fit him Ifor the important (position of .assistant deputy minister?

No particular training, but Mr. Vincent is a very well known, intelligent and clever young man, and he will have an opportunity of training in the department before being appointed as deputy head of the department.
How long do you give him training?
He will have about one year.
My hon. friend intends to make him deputy minister?
Yes.
When?
When Mr. Himsworth is superannuated and retires.

When is he going to
be superannuated?
I expect he will be superannuated during the next six months.

Had the minister
nobody in the department as well fitted to succeed as Mr. Vincent, to whom he is extending a year's education?
I consider that Mr. Vincent is fitted to be the next deputy minister.

I did not ask that.
I asked whether there was no one in the department fit for the position.

I am not in a position
to say so.
You do not know?

I would not like to say
there is no one there fit to be deputy minister, but on the other hand I consider Mr. Vincent will be fit to fill the position.
What was his business before?

A lawyer. I consider
that a lawyer can turn into a deputy minister with training.
The minister believes in the special fitness of members of the legal profession. What is the duty of an official in connection with' a distillery?

He has the supervision
[DOT]of the establishment.

The supervision is
exercised by the people who own the distillery?
The officer is there to see that the inland revenue is not defrauded.

In what way does he
supervise?

He weighs the grain
entering, and he keeps track of all operations in the distillery.
Is he supposed to sample any of the goods sent out?

He is supposed to test
the spirit for its strength.
What salary is paid .these officers?	[DOT]

From $1,800 to $2,200 a
year.

Have they to pass
an examination?

A competitive special
class excise examination.

Did Mr. Vincent
pass any examination?

He was not appointed as supervisor. He passed no examination, and he was exempt from passing an examination, having the certificate of a university; at all events, the commission have accepted Mr. Vincent.

What new district
inland revenue inspectors have been appointed during the past year?
Mr. Dumontier of Quebec and Mr. Macdonald.
He was a butcher?

I do not know what he
was, but I am informed he is one of our very best inspectors.
Who says that?
The officer of the department who receives the report every day.

My information is
that he usually had someone travelling around with him during the past year to teach him what to do.
He is a talented man, because he has learned quickly and easily, and he promises to be one of our best inspectors.

Does the minister
regard examinations as being of any special value in the case of those who are appointed inspectors?
In principle I consider it very important to have examinations,
What about the practice?
Mr. Macdonald's appointment is an exception, and there is in the regulations a special provision for such exceptions.
How many have you appointed inspectors who have not qualified by examination?

Mr. Macdonald is the
only one.
How did you find out the qualifications of this very estimable gentlemen, who was in the victualling trade?
I was informed by one oi my colleagues that he was intelligent and active, and I took his word. He turned out to be a good officer.

My information is
that this gentleman in performing his duty in the Maritime provinces has been accompanied continually by some one who had passed an examination.
I am informed, no.

Does the minister
mean to say that on certain occasions Mr. Macdonald was not accompanied by some officer of the department? I know that he was.
He was accompanied by the Dominion inspector of tobacco for six weeks.
Then why did you say he was not?
No man could be expected to do that work if he did not get instructions at the start.

Could the minister not have selected from the department an officer who had special technical knowledge and training, who could go around and do that work, without it being necessary for some one to accompany him?

I am told all these gentlemen have to be instructed in their duties.
I am told he could not do the work.

I know Mr. Macdonald could not do it, because every one knows that the Department of Inland Revenue is a highly technical one, with regard to the collection of inland revenue and the complicated provisions in reference to excise duty. Most men would have to give a longer period of time to the study of these questions in order to understand them. The minister knows that the only reason he appointed Mr. Macdonald, who was engaged in the meat business in the city of St. John, was because he was an active politician. The minister says Mr. Macdonald is intelligent, and most men who come from the Maritime provinces are intelligent, as to which I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce will bear me out.
There are enough exceptions to prove the rule.

To say that because this gentleman was intelligent is sufficient to entitle him to be inspector, in connection with special and technical work, is incredible. Is the minister going to appoint any more officers of that kind, just because one of his confreres ask him to?
In due time I will consider the question.
Did not you consider it yet?
Mr. Macdonald was recommended to me as a good man, and I have no regret for having appointed him.

Well, the Minister
of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) was very insistent?
No.

And you would not have appointed Mr. Macdonald if it had n.*t bi en that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries insisted upon your doing so?
Mr. NANTEL.: I do not say iso. I would not have appointed him without having taken great care to appoint a good man.
The minister would not have appointed him had it not been that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries insisted upon it?

The Minister of Marine
and Fisheries recommended Mr. Macdonald.
And he insisted upon his appointment?
I do not say that he insisted strongly, but he recommended Mr. Macdonald. I took the word of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I think that I have made a good appointment.

The minister should be frank. I am discussing this matter very frankly with him. The minister knows that he had representations from officers of his department throughout the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick impressing upon him that he should promote some of the men who had spent long years in the service -and who were qualified by examination. The minister received those representations ?
I admit that I received representations that some officer should be promoted. I do not remember the names, but I have received representations from some of the officers in Nova Scotia.

Certainly. The minister will also admit that in the ordinary course of the business of his department he would have made a promotion, had it not been that the political friends of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries Had a man whom they wanted to put in this position, that this man was intelligent and therefore the minister disregarded the others.

If Mr. Macdonald had
not been strongly recommended by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, a gentleman upon whom I rely entirely, I would, before appointing him, have got information to convince me that he was a man fit for the position, and I would have taken all precautions to give him the opportunity of qualifying for the position.
You would not disregard the principle of promotion?
No.
Does not the minister believe that in his department it is a good thing to promote the men who have shown themselves to 'be capable?

Certainly, I admit that,
but that rule carries its exceptions.

And you would
have done that in this case, but for the pressure brought to bear by the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries?

I happen to know the
gentleman who has been appointed to this position. I know that he is a first-class man in every particular.
Very intelligent man, the minister says.
Which is proof of his intelligence. I know that he is a first-class man in every way, well deserving of the position, and a man who will fill it in a most respectable manner.

Better than one of
the men who had grown up in the work and who knew all about it?
Is my hon. friend always so anxious with regard to promotions in the service?

Oh, deal with this
case.

This anxiety of his, it
appears to me, has come too late in life. It has not always been that men have been promoted from the service itself.

In the Inland
Revenue.

And it is not always a
good thing, even then, because the men within the service may not always be competent for the position. At any rate, in this case, however great a wrench it may be to my hon. friend to hear that the promotion has not been from the service, the minister has got in the person of Mr. Macdonald one of the best officials in that particular department or any other department of the Civil Service.

Under what section of the
Act was Mr. Vincent admitted to the department without examination?

Mt. Vincent was admitted to the department under section 21 of the Civil Service Act. Mr. Vincent is a university graduate, and before appointing him I took steps to secure the consent of the Civil Service Commission.
5 p.m. Wliat js the position?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Assistant deputy minister.
The minister states that this man in the course of a year is to be promoted to the position of deputy minister; is that correct?
Yes.
Who occupies the position of deputy minister at the present time?
Mt. Himsworth.
How long has Mr. Himsworth been in the department?
About forty-six years.
How old is he at the present time?
Sixty-six years.
What has been the home or residence of Mr. Vincent, the man who has been appointed to the department already, and who is to be appointed deputy minister?
Ottawa.
How long has he resided in Ottawa?
He has been in Ottawa for many years. I do not know exactly how long. 1 am told that he was born in Ottawa.
Did he practise his profession as an attorney in Ottawa?
He practised in Ottawa.
In company with any one?
In 'company with Mr. Seguin.
Doing business in Ottawa?
Yes.
Did he ever run any election?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not so many as my hon. friend.
But I won my elections; he did not win his.

Had the fact that
Mr. Vincent was the partner of a son-inlaw of my hon. friend anything to do with his selection for office?

It was not for that reason that he was appointed. I really think my hon. friend should not ask such a question. Mr. Vincent was strongly recommended by friends. He ran an election, as has been stated; but the point is that he is considered perfectly qualified for his present position.
My hon. friend does not seem hard to satisfy.
I do not know whether my hon. friend wishes to be disagreeable to me-
Let the hon. minister not get excited; we have been treating him very nicely so far.

What technical knowledge
did Mr. Vincent possess to entitle him to admission to the Civil Service without examination?
I told my hon. friend that the Civil Service Commission considered that Mr. Vincent was well qualified for the position that he now fills, and issued its certificate accordingly.
That is not the point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I can tell my hon. friend. Mr. Vincent was appointed assistant deputy minister just as Mr. Gerald Brown and others were appointed assistant deputy ministers without examination under the late Administration. The Civil Service Act provides that persons below the rank of deputy head must be appointed in a certain way, and I have always under-

stood that the Department of Justice construed the statute in the way to which I have alluded. Several illustrations of appointments could be given under the late Administration, and the appointment of Mr. Vincent-which was made on my own recommendation, and not on the recommendation of the Minister of Inland Revenue-was made in that way.
Mr. Vincent received the approval of the Civil Service Commission. Further than that, so far as the facts are concerned, in making the recommendation I was not-aware that he was practising in partnership with Mr. Seguin, nor was Mr. Vincent's name first given me by the Minister of Inland Revenue.

The explanation, while extremely interesting, does not answer the inquiry I made. If the other gentleman who has been referred to was appointed to the position of assistant deputy minister under a section of the law which allows such appointments to be made, I presume there was satisfactory reason for it. I merely asked the minister what was the technical knowledge which Mr. Vincent possessed that justified the minister in making the appointment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A deputy head can be
appointed under the provisions of the Act without examination or technical qualifications.

If the minister says that
the apptfintment was made under section 21-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Wait a moment. I have explained to my bon. friend that under the ruling of the Department of Justice, which was acted on by the late Administration as well as this, assistant deputies had been appointed under the same provision on the ground and for the reason held to be a valid one by the Department of Justice- that the statute included one case as well as the other.

Still, that is not an answer to my question. Section 21 says that persons can be appointed on account of possessing technical knowledge; otherwise an examination must be passed. Now, I want to know what particular technical knowledge Mr. Vincent possessed to enable him to get around that examination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think he had all the
qualifications posessed by the gentleman to whom I have alluded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have explained that the certificate may have been granted under [DOT]section 21, though I am not aware that that was the case. The action of the Government, as I understand it, was taken for the reason and upon the grounds which I have already suggested to the committee.

Would it not be well for the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Inland Revenue to have a consultation as to how Mr. Vincent really came in? The Minister of Inland Revenue says that he recommended the appointment under section 21, but the Prime Minister seems to think it was under some other section. But still my question is not answered. Again,
I ask, what is the technical knowledge possessed by Mr. Vincent to enable him to get around the examination provided for in the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Upon grounds which were held to be satisfactory by the Civil Service Commission.

We have no proof of that.
If there is a report of the Civil Service Commission, will the minister be good enough to lay it on the table?
If the hon. gentleman desires it I can lay the certificate before the committee, but of course, not now.

The Prime Minister assumes that there must have been good reason for this appointment, and I understand that my hon. friend from Richmond is not denying that. We admit that it is a coincidence-perhaps a rather singular one-that Mr. Vincent was recommended by the Prime Minister without the knowledge of the Minister of Inland Revenue-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say it was without his knowledge.

Then, without being
asked to do so.
Mr. BORDEN':	I did not say that, although I think that in fact that was the case. I said I was not aware that there was a partnership with the gentleman who has been mentioned, and that Mr. Vincent's name was not suggested to me by the Minister of Inland Revenue.

Well, that is not very
different from what I said. It is only a singular coincident that the Prime Minister should have recommended a gentleman who had been recommended to him, or suggested to him, first by some person other than the minister at the head of the department.
I presume the Prime Minister has that power, and I am not here to quarrel with any exercise of his rights. It is a singular coincidence, however, that-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not
aware of the terms of the Order in Council.

We are trying _ to find
that out. We are seeking information, but for some reason-I presume a good one we are not succeeding in getting that in-foruuiticn very rapidly. However, that is what we are here for. My hon. friend from R chmond (Mr. Kyte) is trying to find out from the minister what was the peculiar technical knowledge possessed by this gentleman which entitled him to receive the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission without competitive examination. Surely the minister can give that information. This gentleman was a lawyer, as I understand it; I do not care with whom he was in partnership. I am going to assume that he was a good lawyer and also that he possessed some technical knowledge which fitted him for the position in order to get around what was supposed to be the intention of the Civil Service Act. It may be that shrewd lawyers have found a way to drive a coach and four through the Act. As to the appointment of Mr. Gerald Brown some years ago, I think that the right hon. the Prime Minister has used that argument about as frequently as he ought; it is two and a half years since he commenced to fire that across the floor. We have been patiently waiting to hear from the Prime Minister a justification of the conduct of himself and his Minister of Inland Revenue on its .merits. We have failed so far. I do not think the Prime Minister is helping the case of the Minister of Inland Revenue. We have been getting along very nicely with the hon. minister. We have asked many questions and the hon. minister has acquitted himself in a very gentlemanly way indeed, and I think with great ability, and we on this side, I am sure, have been pleased and gratified with the manner in which he has answered our questions. Now, we would like to come down to business and to have the minister state what were the peculiar qualifications which entitled this gentleman to receive the appointment he has received, and this answer, I think, will settle the whole question.

Evidently, Mr. Vincent
would not have been appointed to such a position except on the certificate of the Civil Service Commission. Mr. Vincent

was recommended upon the certificate of the Civil Service 'Commission, which will be produced if my hon. friend so wishes.

Do I understand the
minister to say that Mr. Vincent's qualifications for the position were submitted to the commission, and that these will be laid before that committee?

Mr. Vincent was well
known by both commissioners; he put his case before the commission, and the commission came to the conclusion that he was qualified for the position. The certificate issued by the commission in favour of Mr. Vincent will be laid before the committee.

An answer given to a question recently by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) shows that the number of appointments in the different departments under section 21 of the Civil Service Act since the present Government came into power is extremely large. Section 21 appears to be a wide-open gate through which applicants for positions may enter the Government service without examination. I think the time has come for the members of this House to scrutinize closely the qualifications of applicants for positions by virtue of which they are appointed without examination. The Chairman will, I am sure, pardon my curiosity, as I have in mind a number of persons who have boon appointed under this section.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	I would like to hear
that section read again.

Section 21 is as follows:
If the deputy head reports that the knowledge and ability requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head of, the department based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination and without reference to the age limit, provided the said person obtains from the commission a certificate, to be given with or without examination, as is determined by the regulations of the commission, that he possesses the requisite knowledge and ability and is duly qualified as to health, character and habits.
It will be observed that a report in writing is also required from the deputy head; I presume the hon. minister will produce the report in writing furnished by the deputy head in this case.

My recollection of the Act is that the certificate of the deputy

head as well as the certificate of the commission is required. I take it that the certificate of the deputy head would be the more important one, and I have no doubt that the hon. minister will be able to give the committee the report of the deputy head as well as the report of the commission.

I am willing to produce
the recommendation of the deputy head as well as the certificate of the commission.

The hon. minister said
that he was under the impression that this appointment was made under section 44 of the Act. I presume that was a mistake?
I was under the impression that that was the section, but evidently I was mistaken.

Looking over the
Auditor General's Report, I find that a large number of the officers employed by the minister are temporary employees. On page I-13, for instance, the following temporary employees are mentioned: For Saskatchewan, temporary exciseman, J. J. Libbey; High River, R. E. Sobey; Lacombe, J. McKenty; Medicine Hat, J. H. Collier; Pincher Creek, J. H. Schofield; Stettler, W. B. Gray; Red Deer, W. H. Cottingham; Taber, H. P. Monroe; Vermilion, M. A. Brimacombe; Moosejaw, W. O. Lowe; Estevan, D. R. Davies; North Battleford, A. M. Panton; Swift Current, R. W. Edmanson; Weyburn, W. J. H. McGowan.
It is rather striking that the hon. minister has so many temporary officers in the different provinces. Will the hon. minister explain this, and tell the committee why he does not make permanent appointments in the places mentioned?

One of the reasons is that many of these officers attend to unimportant factories, tobacco factories for instance, in small places. They are appointed temporarily at small salaries, and as they have an opportunity of devoting their time to other occupations, they do take the temporary office.

Do I understand that even in small towns where there are only tobacco or cigar factories, these temporary employees could, by passing the necessary examination, become permanent officers, or are they always left on the temporary list?

Sometimes they do not
care to pass the examinations because they have time to devote to other business, but

they can be permanently appointed if they pass the necessary examination.

In the town of Farn'ham, for instance, where there is a cigar factory [DOT]conducted by a man by the name of Ruel, a temporary employee was appointed under the late Government to collect the excise" from this factory. Of course he was replaced by another officer when the change of Government took place, but what I want to know is whether an employee who is earning a very small salary, say $50 a year or less, for collecting the revenue from a small factory, would be entitled to pass an examination, and, if so, whether the department would be obliged to appoint him to a better position.
Not obliged to employ him, but I may employ him, especially if he is an efficient officer.

In connection with the extra duty pay at large distilleries and other factories, those employed, as I understand, are already receiving large salaries, $1,400 and more per year. This item is extra duty pay to these same officers. I see the item is the same as was voted last year and the year before, so that this is evidently an old system. Has the minister considered increasing their regular pay instead of paying these extra amounts every year as extra duty pay?

I would support the idea that it would be much better for the minister to increase the salaries of these officials 'by an amount which would be sufficient to cover the extra allowance per annum for this purpose and thus avoid the trouble of keeping their time and passing small bills, etc.
All of these excisemen are not called upon to work longer hours. I am told that this practice is the result of many years of experience, and that it is found to be the best system to work on.

When the minister comes to the vote for the adulteration of food and inspection of food, would he kindly be prepared to give some information as to the number of officials in his employ who are charged with the analysis of different foods and commodities, which I think is far the most important part of his department? In my judgment, the department is doing good work. I would like to see it extended. It is of the greatest importance that the department should double or quadruple the number of exam-90
inations they are now making of food, essences, fertilizers, and all these things that enter into the ordinary lives of the people. I had an illustration not long ago in reference to fertilizers, an important thing in the Maritime provinces. A concern had sent out hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of fertilizer under a certain guarantee. The department analysed samples, and found them all very far below the guarantee. That meant a loss to many people and may result in litigation.

We have now only one office, in Ottawa, under the control of Dr. McGill; but during last summer I had an Order in Council passed to establish three new offices, in Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver. In the Estimates there is an item of $21,000 for this purpose. At the head of each of these new offices we intend to put one of our best analysts from Ottawa. We have had great difficulty in finding good men, but Dr. McGill has gone to great trouble and has succeeded in training some very good young men whom he intends to put at the head of these new laboratories.

Sydney is a centre of industry and a rapidly growing city, and the cost of living there is exceedingly high. Last year, while a friend of ours was chief officer in the excise in Sydney, I asked for an increase in his salary. He, unfortunately, passed away and a new man was appointed in his place, a friend of the present Administration and an exceedingly capable man. I congratulate the minister upon the appointment of such an efficient officer as Mr. McKeen. He is an educated gentleman, a man of wide experience, and the minister might travel far and wide before he would find another equally capable man. Living in Sydney, as he is obliged to do, a man of family and no longer a young man, although he is not a political friend of mine, still he is a very close personal friend and a man of exceptional ability, and I would like to bring to the notice of the minister the fact that $900 a year is not enough for a man to live on in Sydney and to maintain himself and his family in the manner in which a gentleman occupying that position is obliged to do. I hope that before long, if not at once, the minister will increase that salary to something like $1,500 a year, which would be the least that a man could expect to live on in that city and hold such an office as Mr. McKeen is holding.

None.

Three.

breweries or distilleries in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick?

At St. John and Fairville.

In Nova Scotia there are two cigar manufacturers and one tobacco manufacturer.
The minister made no reply to my question in regard to Mr. McKeen.

Mr. McKeen receives only $900. He has only been appointed within six months. He is the collector at Glace Bay. I am inclined to increase his salary, but we generally expect an officer shall serve longer than six months before his salary is increased. As soon as he has been in office long enough I shall certainly increase his salary, but I cannot undertake to give him $1,500 unless I am authorized to do so by the law, which, I expect, will be accepted by the House, authorizing an increase in the salaries of all the officers of the department. I consider myself that the officers of the department are underpaid. But as the law is now, I am bound by the regulations. If I increased the salary of Mr. McKeen to $1,500 I would be called upon to increase the salaries of all the other officers in the same position.

I should think that his salary ought to be increased very much, and I hope the Minister will take that into his consideration.

All these officers in the western provinces are on the same footing. They receive about the same salary besides their provisional allowance. The salary is regulated by the classification of the division. We have several divisions according to the importance of the work as indi-

cated by the amount collected, and the salary is proportioned to the amount collected.

Is not that a small
salary for such an important position?

I believe that the salaries
of all these officers are too small, and I expect to be able to put them all on the same footing.

I expect this session.

What is the reason for the increase?

It is due to increase of operations. This includes the expenses of all our inspectors or other officers who are obliged to make inspections. For instance, we have Mr. Barrett at Winnipeg, who is obliged to go elsewhere to inspect distilleries, warehouses, etc.

Would it not be cheaper to have these officers stationed in the respective districts? That necessitates a waste of time and' heavy travelling expenses. Instead of having all the officers in the districts of Halifax and Pictou, they could be distributed over the province.

There is a collector and an inspector in each district, and the latter .inspects all the officers under him. There is a chief inspector, Mr. Barrett, at Winnipeg, who inspects the malt houses and breweries.
If it was reported that an illicit still was being operated, say, at Glace Bay, an officer would have to go there to investigate.
If such a thing should happen a report would be made to the collector of the division at Pictou, who would send an officer and take proceedings.
