Some time ago a new regulation was promulgated by the Department of Inland Revenue compelling the adoption of a new scale, technically termed the beam scale, instead of the spring scale. I am advised by many of my constituents that this new regulation will operate as a great hardship upon many people. In the first place, a number of hardware merchants are supplied with the
style of scale that has been in use for a great many years.
Further, a great number of householders have purchased the old style of scale; and to compel them to cease the use of it and to adopt another form will, I am told, be an unnecessary hardship. Why was this new regulation passed by the department, and is not the scale that is now in use and that has been in use for some years for household purposes particularly, as good a scale as the beam scale for such purposes?

The idea of this regulation is to discard the spring scale, which does not give entire satisfaction. We have discussed the question for many months. Since I have been in office, we have met most of the interests concerned, and we have rea hed the conclusion that the spring scale should be discarded.
Who are the interested people in Canada, outside of the users of the scales?
The users-retailers and others. There are some exceptions to the regulation.
Who are the manufacturers of scales in Canada?

Canadian manufacturers
and American manufacturers are interested in this matter. The regulation was to prevent the flooding of the Canadian market with very cheap American scales.
Is the minister trying to help the Canadian manufacturer or the public?
The protection of the public was the first purpose, and the Canadian manufacturer against the American manufacturers, who were flooding the country with cheap and inaccurate scales.
Did the Canadian manufacturers urge this change?
Yes.
Were they in favour of it?
Certainly.
Did any retailer or con sumer ever approach the minister and ask for the change?

We considered that it was
for the protection of the consumers to compel the retailers to keep accurate scales.

I do not believe that the people are interested in that direction whatever. It may be true that the beam scale is more accurate than the spring scale, but for domestic and household purposes I believe that the consumers would prefer the spring scale to the beam scale. The former is sufficiently accurate and much more convenient.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Is there anything to prevent the consumer from using
5 p.m. any scale he chooses? This is only where people are selling by
weight.

The complaint of my hon. friend is the first that we have received against the new regulation. I will certainly take it into consideration, especially if there are many more complaints. I consider that the new regulation is required and is in the interest of the consumer.
Do I understand the regulation to mean that hereafter a dealer cannot sell a spring scale to a user, if the latter wishes to buy one?

The dealer can sell a
spring scale, but not a cheap inaccurate one.
What can he sell?
A good spring scale approved by the inspector of the department.
And manufactured in Canada?
What was the purpose of the regulation? How is it worded, when it operates only against a low grade spring scale?

I shall be glad to read
the regulation, but it is very technical. There are certain exceptions. The spring scale may be inspected and stamped for the weighing of ice only-that is the exception -when found to comply with the regulations. All the scales are under the control of the Inspector of Weights and Measures, and it is the only way to control them and to protect the public. If these spring scales are accurate, they are considered legal and stamped by the inspector. The idea is to discard gradually the spring scales when considered inaccurate by the inspector of the department.
They may be abolished?

That is the idea at all
events. This is the first complaint that the department has received on behalf of the

spring scale. If we receive many- such complaints, we will try to ascertain if our attempt to protect the public is more objectionable than the grievance which we are trying to remedy.

I am not very conversant with the regulation or its possible effect, but I know that the department has had protests from dealers in regard to this regulation. I have in my possession a copy of a letter sent to the department by a Halifax dealer, with whom I had a personal interview less than a week ago, when he informed me that he thought it was a great and unnecessary hardship upon the public.

I am informed that,
since this new regulation came into effect, we have received a few letters from hardware merchants.

The hardware merchants say that this regulation has been made at the request of a Toronto manufacturer of scales, and that the department up to date has given to the public no good reason for the change. There should be some way of informing the public as to the justification of this regulation.

It has been proven to
my satisfaction and to that of the chief inspector of weights and measures that the cheap imported spring scales are not accurate, and in order to protect the public against fraud-
Is there a definition of a cheap scale in your regulation?
No.
Is it optional with the officers to say whether or not a certain spring scale can be continued in use, or does it say that only scales of a certain make can be used?
It is practically under the control of the chief inspector. [DOT]

I am informed that
householders, women particularly, of late years, have begun-and very properly-to use spring scales to test the weight of purchases made. These need not be finely accurate; they afford a substantial test of the accuracy of the scales used by the dealers who supply goods. To use a beam scale for a household test of this kind would be unnecessary. I am informed that this regulation prohibits the use of spring scales for domestic purposes, and I wish to know whether that is correct or not.

142r
An inaccurate scale in a household cannot be used to test the scale of the merchant.
But will you allow the dealer in scales to sell them?

Not if they are inaccurate.
It is not right to subject the trader's scales to the test of a cheap and inaccurate scale.

But there surely must
be some better explanation of the regulation than the minister has given. There should be general statutory power given to the Inland Revenue Department to put out of commission any inaccurate scale, but surely the regulation does not say merely that the dealers may not sell inaccurate scales. There must be a definition of the class of scales.

At all events this is a new regulation, and should it prove defective it will be very easy to cancel it. But we consider it a good regulation.
Mr-. MACLEAN: We import a large number of these scales from England, and they are considered very satisfactory for household use. If the home manufacturer tells the department that they are inaccurate and they are all forbidden, the dealer who has purchased them will lose.
We do not accept manufacturers' statements; we test the scales ourselves.

Does the minister say
that he regulates scales used for domestic purposes? Surely, there is a difference between a scale used in a grocery for the weighing of goods to the public and the scale used in the household.

Every scale in Canada
should be inspected.

Am I prohibited from
having a scale in my own house without having it inspected ?

The law provides that
every scale shall be inspected.
Then, it is contrary to the law for me to have a scale for my own use without inspection?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It must have been inspected before it was bought.

That is, it must hare
been inspected in the dealer's shop, but the officers do not go to a private house to inspect scales used merely for household purposes?

They are inspected in
the hands of the manufacturer or importer.

Complaint has been
made by grocers in the part of Nova Scotia where I live that officers are Inspecting their scales more frequently now than: in former years, and that they are compelled to pay the inspection fee. Has any change been made in the regulations? And what fee is charged' by the officer who makes the test? How are these fees levied,, and are they levied more often than formerly. Has the minister received any complaints from the trade on this account?'

The spring scale loses
its accuracy more quickly than another and these scales must be inspected every year, while the others are inspected every two years. The fee for such inspection is: 50 cents on a scale up to 30 pounds.
The minister refers toscales used in weighing out goods for the-public, not to scales used in the household.

The scales in private
houses are not inspected, but they must be inspected before they are sold.

They must bear the-
Government stamp. But what the member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is getting at is that under the regulations dealers are prohibited from selling these scales.
The idea is to gradually cause inaccurate scales to be discarded- the cheap imported scales.

That is my inquiry.
What justification is there for such action-by the department? Was the judgment sound that led to the passing of such a regulation?
The reports of the chief inspector and the general experience of the department have led to the conclusion that this is a sound policy.

I can readily understand' that there may be some reason for discarding these scales if they become inaccurate shortly after they are sold, but I cannot' understand why they should be discarded after they have been examined' by the inspectors of the department, either in the hands of the importers or in the-hands of the manufacturers. The minister will understand, of course, that in private families beam scales are not used; they are too cumbersome and too expensive. I think this regulation will place a hardship-

on the housewife who requires a small scale for her own use. Small domestic scales are used for two purposes: first, to test the weight of the various articles bought in the stores, and secondly to weigh at the'' door of the house the products of the farmer who goes around selling his goods. With all due deference to what the minister has told the committee, I think that the department, if it has decided to discard these scales, has made a mistake. Certainly, if upon testing a scale of any description they find it to be inaccurate, it should be discarded, but if a scale is accurate, no matter what its make may be, the department should not outline a plan to put it gradually out of existence.

These cheap spring scales are considered to be inaccurate, and the department considers that the result of the effort to prohibit them will be that another cheap and accurate scale will be put on the market.

When these scales are first examined, the inspector can tell immediately whether or not they are accurate. If the scale is not accurate, let him put it out of existence by instructing the importer or the manufacturer that he must not sell it. But surely it is penalizing the public to say, because some of the scales may be inaccurate, that none of them shall be sold.

Some of the cheap scales which are imported from the United States are so poorly made that they become inaccurate almost immediately. Possibly that is the reason why the Department of Inland Revenue had the regulations changed in order to provide that the scales shall be inspected every year instead of every two years.

But the regulation does not discriminate between good scales and bad scales; it applies with equal force to the first-class spring scale imported from England and the poor scale imported from the United States.

All spring scales are not discarded. Some are good, and some are bad; the Post Office Department has been notified by the Department of Inland Revenue that some of the scales in use in the Post Office Department would have to be discarded because of their having become inaccurate in a short time. Canadian firms are now manufacturing scales just about as cheap as, but much better 
and much more accurate, than those imported from the United States.

General tell the committee what is the meaning and effect of this regulation?

The effect of the
regulation is to stamp out .scales which will deceive the public.

Whether used by private

They have the right to dispose of whatever stock they have on hand.

In the papers showing the work done by the preventive officers at Pictou, I find that the reports are al- [DOT] most all in stereotyped form, simply saying that he visited the different towns in the country and that he made inquiries from reputable people and could find no violation of the law. These reports, as they stand, are of no value. The payment of salaries to these preventive officers, judging by these reports, is a useless expense.

I frankly admit that
these reports are not as perfect as they might" be if prepared by a lawyer, but the present system is certainly better than the one before this system was introduced, because formerly officers gave no sign of life except when it was time for us to pay their salaries.

That is about what
they are doing now.
I shall give consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend.

The minister is
very oily about this thing, but his suggestion that he has inaugurated some wonderful system by which the people get some return for the money expended is too

ridiculous. I was suggesting that the department should send out to officers blank forms stating what places and what stores they visited, and the people from whom they got information. It is ridiculous that public officers should be drawing salaries for sending reports of this kind.

I ask my hon. friend if
it is really not a little better to have such a letter, stating that the officer is still alive, than to have the old system under which we received news of these men only when they were asking for payment.

The supervising collector for each district was expected to give his attention to the performance of their duties by the men under him. The department held the supervisor of the district responsible for the men under him. If my hon. friend regards these documents as reports I can only say to him that they are the most ludicrous reports that ever went into a Government.

Mr. J. T. Dagneau has

Mr. Desjardins.
Mr. Desjardins is in Ei-rnouski. Was there another appointment made in Gaspe also to replace Mr. Bujeaud?

Mr. Desjardins receives
only $200, Mr. Dagneau $450, and Mr. Myles $200.

But these men do not
give all their time to their offices as inspectors of weights and measures.
I understand that he does not give all his time to this work. *
Why should he be paid $450 while Myles gets only $200 and Desjardins $300?

Because Mr. Myles has
less to inspect.

I am told that he has
less to inspect.

The result is that these

With respect to Mr. Caldwell I would like to know whether an investigation was held and whether or not he was given an opportunity to defend himself.	'
No investigation has been given to Mrs* Caldwell. We had received solemn declarations stating that Mr. Caldwell had been a partisan and that is the reason for his being dismissed.

Does not the minister
think that he should have been given a hearing? Mr. Caldwell was supposed to be a respectable man?

I have no doubt that Mr. Caldwell is a respectable man, but my information, sworn to in these affidavits, convinced me that he was guilty of the offence that he was charged with and I sanctioned his dismissal.
What kind of a Liberal is a Liberal dog?
I do not know, I am sure.

The minister is a lawyer, a distinguished member of his profession, and as such does he not think it would only have been common justice to have given this man a hearing or an opportunity to meet those who made these charges against him? The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), who has been looked upon as the forerunner of the movement in connection with dismissals in my constituency, gave some of those against whom charges were made there, a chance to be heard. He even sent certain forms for them to fill out, and he gave them an opportunity of saying something before the axe fell. But in this case no opportunity was given at all. I am sorry that this is so because Mr. Caldwell was one of the best men in the service of the hon. gentleman in that county. Mr. Caldwell, was appointed to replace Mr. Kelly, father of the present local member for the constituency. Mr. Caldwell had given good service to the department. I give you my word that I never knew Mr. Caldwell to take the least interest in politics; I never asked him to canvass for me or to give me any assistance whatever. I frankly told the minister that last year, when he spoke to me about the matter. Mr. Bujeaud went on the platform and took his official life in his hands. In the case of Caldwell an injustice has been done, because the minister would not give him an opportunity of meeting the charges. I think the feeling of the entire people of the county is to that effect. There is one affidavit, outside of that of Mr. Ross, against whom I have nothing to say. Mr. Mills is a lawyer and he will be able to take the responsibility for what he says. The second affidavit is one to which I wish to call the attention of the minister, because it says that on the 17th of September, 1912, he heard Mr. Caldwell canvassing at the door of the Presbyterian church in favour of the Liberal party. Well, we all know what it is in the country, when people meet at the door of the church they talk about different things, and to charge a man with canvassing, in a case like that, is a very general charge to make. Under all the circumstances, I am sorry for the reputation of the minister that opportunity was not given Mr. Caldwell to meet the charges. So far as the new appointments are concerned, I know nothing of them; exfcept that Mr. Desjardins is of Sayabec, in the county of Rimouski. I know nothing about Mr. Myles except that he is a strong Conservative and belongs to Gaspd comity. I am very familiar with Mr. John T. Dagneau, and he is about the strongest partisan on the Conservative side, that we have in the county of Bonaventure. When the Estimates come before us for the Post ^Office Department, I will be able to show that in connection with the removal of a large number of postmasters in Bonaventure county, and with regard to the work of getting evidence against them, and

all the work generally of the Conservative organization in the whole western part of the county, it was carried on by Mr. John T. Dagneau, who was afterwards appointed postmaster at Robitaille. He was appointed to that office on the ground that he had been dismissed in 1896. During the time he was postmaster at Robitaille, he secured a second position in the Inland Revenue Department, and he passed over the post office to his brother. What I want to call the attention of the minister to, in simple justice, is, that if these men have been dismissed because they were active partisans, he should keep his eye upon Mr. John T. Dagneau, who is the strongest partisan we have in the county of Bonaventure. In the case of John T. Dagneau, when the time came to appoint him postmaster at Robitaille, I wrote to the Postmaster General and asked that Mr. Quinn, a very respectable old man, who was the postmaster at Robitaille, should be given an opportunity of being heard before he was dismissed, because it was notorious that Mr. Quinn had taken no part in politics. The minister replied he was sorry he could not give Mr. Quinn a hearing, because he had decided to appoint Mr. Dagneau, on the ground that it was a reinstatement, as he held the office previous to 1896. Immediately after that came the new appointment of Mr. Dagneau as preventive officer. I think, under all the circumstances, that Mr. Dagneau has had a fair share of the patronage and has been well paid by the Conservative party for what he has done. What I am sorry to learn, for the nominee of my hon. friend from Rimouski, is, that his protege receives only $200 and the protege of my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Gauthier) receives only $300, while Mr. John T. Dagneau, who has a smaller territory to cover, and who has been able to juggle the postmastership of Robitaille between himself and his brother, has managed to get out of the Department of Inland Revenue $450. Out of curiosity I would like the minister to give me a report from Mr. Dagneau as to what he has done since he has been in office.

1 would like to learn from the Minister of Inland Revenue whether Mr. Caldwell was dismissed because he was preaching Liberalism or because he was simply preaching before the door of the Presbyterian church. So far the matter has not been made clear.
The affidavit says he was canvassing before the Presbyterian church door.	'	! j

That was preaching
out of church.
I suppose he was accused of preaching in favour of the Liberal party, but is there a report from Mr. Dagneau?

There is not a report,
here but I will make inquiries.

The net result is that instead of the country paying $500 per annum for these services as was paid under the Liberal Government, we are now paying $950 for exactly the same services, and this is merely a reward for partisans. I have no doubt that my hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) will admit that Mr. Desjardins is a good Conservative. I know that_ Mr. Myles is. end I am quite sure that Mr. Dagneau is. I wish to repeat that in the case of Mr. Caldwell a real injustice has been committed.

I congratulate the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) on his frankness in acknowledging that his friend, Mr. Bujeaud, did more than enough to justify his dismissal. As a matter of fact, Mr. Bujeaud took an active part in every general election that was held in the county of Rimouski of late years. In 1908, he even,
I believe, took a hand in the electoral fray at Rimouski, and he should at that very time have been dismissed by his party, had they applied the principle just laid down by the hon. member for Bonaventure in regard to Mr. Dagneau.
As regards the charge made by the hon. member for Bonaventure that this Government has increased the amount which the country is called upon to pay towards the inspection of weights and measures, by appointing three inspectors instead of those formerly in- charge, I may state that he is mistaken and that the expenditure is in no way increased. Thus, Mr. Bujeaud was getting $400 per annum, and at the time of his dismissal, Mr. Desjardins, of Sayabec, was appointed to take his place, jointly with a man in the county of Gaspe, and up to date they have been paid $200 each per annum. However, I understand that for the coming year Mr. Desjardins' salary will be increased, and that is only fair, for he has two counties to go through, while Mr. Dagneau and the inspector for Gaspe have only one county to look after.
Excise-Rental, fuel, travelling expenses, $55,000.
What revenue has been received from the inspection of electric meters?

Does that include gas
meters as [DOT]well as electric meters?
Electric meters only.

The total estimated cost of that service is only $73,950. Does it not occur to the minister that the department has no right to make a profit out of the inspection of these meters? It is quite a heavy tax. As a matter of fact these meters are only inspected about once in every five years, and generally only when the consumers request it. It does seem to me that when the law of the land is that these meters should be inspected the Government should stand a proportion at least of the expense.
The amount collected has been $74,803; the expense of inspection is $33,760; the expense of standard instruments and maintenance of equipment $8,945, leaving a balance of $32,120.

Which goes into the
consolidated revenue fund?
We are obliged to spend $12,000 for the laboratory and instruments.

The instruments do
not wear out so rapidly that you have to spend $12,000 in each year. You 'have made a profit of $32,000 on this transaction, which is about 100 per cent. Does it not appeal to the minister that the consumers should contribute $32,000 to the revenue of the country over and above the amount required to carry on the service? That is a direct taxation on the consuming public. Three or four years ago there was quite a large reduction made in the cost of inspection but the number of meters have increased so rapidly that this has now become a revenue-producing scheme.

I am pleased to be
blamed for having a surplus, but perhaps next year we will have a deficit and we will also meet with blame for that. These technical officers receive very low pay and believing as I do that they should have a larger salary, I will take into consideration the observations of my hon. friend.

I do not know whether
or not it is a fact that the officers are underpaid, but realizing as I do that it requires well trained and almost technical men to perform this duty, if it is necessary to pay higher salaries I will find no fault. I think we have only one officer of this kind in the province of New Brunswick, and I do not
see how that officer can be engaged more than two or three months in the year m actual work, because one officer will inspect for a year all the meters in a town, in a couple of days. I am not saying that the officers do not do their duty, but I do say there should not be this very heavy charge upon the public. So much more electricity is being consumed now than formerly that the minister can very well afford to cut these by one-quarter and still cover all the.expenses of inspection.
Mr. KYTE * Before the committee rose at six o'clock the minister promised to bring down the report of his deputy minister as to the special qualifications of Mr. Vincent for the position to which he has been called in the department.
Here is the report of the Civil Service Commissioners
I asked for the report of the deputy minister of the department which is required under the provisions of the Act.

I have not the report of
the deputy minister, but I have the certificate signed by Mr. Shortt and Mr. Laro-chelle.

The important part is the
report of the deputy head of the department. Section 21 of the Civil Service Act reads:
II the deputy head reports that the knowledge and ability requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical, or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head of the department, based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination-
The minister, therefore, was unable to act until he had a report from the deputy head and that is the report I would like to have.

Here is the certificate of the Civil Service Commissioners:
The Civil Service Commissioners have had under consideration an application from the Minister of Inland Revenue to issue a certificate of qualification under the provisions of sections 21 and 33 of the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, in favour of Mr. J. U. Vincent with a view to his appointment as Assistant Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue in subdivision A of the first division at an initial salary of $3,300, being $500 in excess of the minimum salary prescribed for tnat subdivision of the service.
The commissioners understand that Mr. Vincent's proposed appointment to the position of assistant Deputy Minister is intended to afford him an opportunity to become familiar with the administration of the department in order that

the Government may later appoint him to the position of Deputy Minister ui inland Revenue, an appointment which does not require the accompaniment of a certificate from the Civil [DOT]Service Commission. Under these conditions, and considering that the professional qualifications of Mr. Vincent as a lawyer of considerable experience would render him qualified to fill the position for which he is recommended.
Now, therefore, this is to certify, pursuant to the provisions of section 21 of the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, that, in their opinion, Mr. J. U. Vincent possesses me requisite knowledge and ability, and is duly qualified as to ihealth, character and habits for appointment to the position of assistant Deputy Minister in .subdivision A of the first division of the Department of Inland Revenue. The commissioners further certify, pursuant to the provisions [DOT]of section 33 of the Act, that Mr. Vincent possesses the exceptional qualifications required for the performance of the duties of such position.
Dated at the office of the Civil Service Commission of Canada this 16th day of August, 1913.
Adam Shortt,
M. G. Larochelle, Commissioners.

The recommendation of the [DOT]Civil Service Commission is one that would issue as a matter of course. As for setting forth any special qualifications possessed by Mr. Vincent, it shows, on the contrary, that he was appointed to the department to use it as a training school to fit him [DOT]for the deputyship.
And his health is good?

Yes, a doctor's certificate on that point would have been at least as convincing. Under the law the Civil Service Commission could not act until they had the report of the deputy minister setting forth the technical qualifications that Mt. Vincent possessed. That being received, as I have said, the report of the Civil Service Commission would follow as a matter of course. But the report shows that he is to be paid $3,300 and given an appointment that will give him opportunity [DOT]to team for the position of deputy minister. I submit that the minister has not brought down the information that the committee desires. I think he has no reason to complain of the treatment he has received from this side during the progress of Supply. I would ask the minister to suspend further consideration of his Estimates until the report of the deputy minister is brought down.
I can only produce what I have.
Is there a report from the deputy minister on the subject?

No, there is a recommendation signed by the minister, as follows:	-
The undersigned has the honour to recommend that Mr. J. U. Vincent, barrister, of the city of Ottawa, he, from the 1st October, 1913, appointed, under the provisions of section 21 of the Civil Service Act of 1908, to the position of assistant Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue vice Mr. William Himsworth, promoted to the position of Deputy Minister, at a salary of $2,800 per annum, and that, under section 33 of the same Act, he be paid from the 1st October, an additional salary of $500 per annum, making his total salary $3,300, he being possessed of exceptional Qualifications required for the performance of the duties of such position.
Hereunto attached is the certificate of the Civil Service Commission in support of such appointment.
W. B. Nantel, Minister of Inland Revenue.

I submit that there is no legal authority for the appointment of Mr. Vincent in this position. Under the Civil Service Act he should have submitted himself to examination by the commission unless he possessed special technical qualifications to fit him for the position to which he was to be appointed. The appointment under section 21 could not have been made at all except upon the recommendation of the deputy head of the department setting forth his special technical qualifications. The minister himself has to admit that fto such report has been made by the deputy head-nothing more than a recommendation that Mr. Vincent be appointed to this position. I can well understand that the deputy minister with pressure brought to bear upon him by the minister and some of his colleagues would sign such a recommendation. But it does not comply with section 21 of the Civil Service Act. So, we are face to face w:th the fact that the present Government, in order to reward its supporters for past political services, will, in defiance of the Civil Service Act and of the established practice in all the departments, dole out positions with from $2,500 to $3,300. I think it is as well the country should understand what is being done by this Government in the matter of driving a coach and four through the clauses of the Civil Service Act. We have had a good deal of criticism in the past on the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side, particularly by members of the present Government, concerning the necessity for Civil Service reform. Truly we have had Civil Service reform with a vengeance since these gentlemen came into power. We have had hundreds and thousands of officials dismissed upon allegations of partisanship though in

fifty per cent of the cases no evidence of partisanship has been adduced and the plain fact is that these men were dismissed so as to provide positions for hungry followers of the Government. The Civil Service Act is defied, the highly-paid Civil Service Commissioners are ignored except that they are asked to act as a stamping machine to certify men to office. If there is a defence for all this on the part of the Minister of Inland Revenue, I am curious to hear what it is. The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) some time ago moved for a return showing the number of those who had been appointed to public office by virtue of section 21 of the Civil Service Act. I do not remember at this moment the number of such appointments, but I venture to say that the case we have unearthed to-night is not an isolated case. We have to-night uncovered what I regard as the greatest scandal in the matter of appointment to public office; and I think it would be well for members on this side to go thoroughly into the appointments listed in the return of those made under section 21.

May I be permitted to add that the very unfortunate part of this whole transaction is the fact that we have had the confession of the Prime Minister that he is the man who made this recommendation. It seems to me it would have been bad enough coming from the Minister of Inland Revenue, but when the Prime Minister himself is the prime mover in violating the law, in appointing men to office without authority, in practically pilfering from the public funds from $2,500 to $3,300 a year, it is so serious that there ought really to be an investigation into the matter. And I want to tell the Minister of Inland Revenue before we separate that if he never did another good thing in this world, he has done well to shoulder off this nefarious transaction upon the Prime Minister.

Is there any
danger of the minister's resigning because of this matter?

The Prime Minister
has himself taken the responsibility for having done this.

We are glad to have
that on record.

After all, I do not
think there is so much ground for complaint in this matter. Of course, if you examine the text of the law and try to put a different 91
construction upon it by reading between the lines, perhaps you may have occasion to find fault with this appointment, as well as with every appointment that has been made by this and the preceding Government.

Do not bother about
that; defend yourself.
Have I said anything to hurt the feelings of my hon. friend?
No, but we are becoming nauseated by continually hearing the answer, 'you are guilty too.'

My hon. friend may
become nauseated or he may not; he will have to take his medicine anyway. He should not get warm over this matter; I am speaking politely about it.
So am I.

The hon. gentleman
is trying to, but he does not succeed very well. This appointment has been made in accordance with the statute. There was no deputy minister at the time, but a recommendation was made by the acting deputy minister to the Civil Service Commission, and they looked into the matter of Mr. Vincent's qualifications for the position. They made their report, and on that report the appointment was based. We are told that we are filtering away public money in doing this; surely there are more grievous charges against the Government than that.

There are, but to say
there are does not minimize the seriousness of this offence.

We have done nothing so very bad after all; my hon. friend has put one construction on the Act and we have put another. The law says that the Civil Service Commission has to recommend the man, and that the recommendation of Council is to be made by the minister upon the report of the deputy head. In this case there was no deputy head, but the acting deputy minister made a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission, which the commissioners approved. Surely there is nothing so very bad in all this; I do not think the appointment of this man has been so irregular as to justify all this trouble. The hon. member for Carleton will have to admit that the Civil Service Commission were consulted, and found that Mr. Vincent possessed the necessary special qualifications. I do not think my hon. friends have much reason to find fault, and I would suggest that we keep to the agreement made at six o'clock to adjourn at ten.

Even if it be after ten o'clock, it is rather hard to let go by an assertion so illogical as that put forward by the hon. Postmaster General. In the first place he says that there was no deputy head and that, therefore, there was nobody to make the necessary recommendation. In that event, nobody should have been recommended; violated was the law by the appointment of a man who was not recommended by the proper official. The very report of the commission shows that the Go\ ernment is taking this man in and schooling him for a year in order to make him ready for the duties of his office. Wny on earth does the Government not appoint a man who does not need any schooling? Why has this country to put up $3,000 to educate a man who does not know enough to occupy the position? Then the Postmaster General says that the man who was appointed had all the necessary recommendations and qualifications; he got the certificate of the acting deputy minister; he got the certificate of the Civil Service Commission, and nothing more was necessary-yet this country is paying $3,300 a year to teach him how to do his work. The whole thing is a farce upon the face of it, and I am surprised that even the Postmaster General should attempt to defend it.
My hon. friend is departing from the question. He says now that this man is being educated or trained for his position.
That is what the report says.

I do not think my
hon. friend will find outside of the public service a man who may not learn something in carrying out the duties of a position in a department so technical as that of Inland Revenue.
Why did they not promote one of the men in the department who knew something about the work?

The Civil Service
Commissioners have been appointed by law to be the judges of the qualifications of persons for appointment to positions in the Government service. They came to the conclusion that the gentleman in this case possessed the necessary qualifications, and I think the hon. member for Carleton has no right to find fault with the Government in respect of his appointment.

My hon. friend knows
that no such recommendation would have been made if the Government had not asked the Civil Service Commission for it. If the Government had asked the commission to pass upon the qualifications of one of the officers of the department, they would have recommended him just as readily.

The Civil Service
Commissioners are not inclined to do things simply because they are told to do them.
Since when.

I am not allowed to speak of the late Government; my hon. friend may become nauseated, but since this Government has come into power we have never had reason to say that the Civil Service Commissioners have been too obliging. For my part, I have been unable to promote deserving men in. my department who were appointed by my friends on the other side simply because Mr. Shortt of the Civil Service Commission thought he knew more about it than the officers of my department. Mr. Shortt does what he considers to be his duty; he does not do this or that simply because he is told to do it. He has a pretty solid head on his shoulders, and he is not to be led into doing anything unless he wants to do it. This being disposed of-
Not yet. I should like to ask the hon. Postmaster General a question.
I have my hands full in dealing with the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton without the hon. member for Pictou butting in.
The matter is not disposed of by any means.

If my hon. friend is not satisfied now I will never try to satisfy him, because it is useless to try to persuade any one who will not be persuaded. As to my hon. friend's remarks that the Civil Service Commision were told to do this-

I did not say that; I will tell my hon. friend what I did say. I said that they had done it because this name had been handed to them. What I am finding fault with is that they handed the name of an outsider and not . the name of some official in the department. I am not saying tnat the commission did this because they were told to do it, but because this was the only name put forward to

them. I do not know what the Civil Service Commission did. I do not know what investigation they made, because unfortunately the report does not contain that information.
Yes, it does.

They practically certify that he was a man in good health and fit physically to occupy the position. I did not hear much more, so my hon. friend is arguing entirely from wrong premises. I cannot understand why it was necessary to violate all the principles of the Act, in order to get in a man who, my hon. friend admits, did not know anything about the department, who had to take a year to be educated about the department. This is the man whose name was sent to the Civil Service Commission when there were plenty of good men in the department who did know the duties intimately, who had been educated for years, who would not have had to go to school for a year at a cost of $3,300, but who possessed all the necessary information, who could have been promoted to occupy the position-and then this affair never would have happened.

The whole difficulty is this, if I understand my hon. friend, that the appointment has been made of a certain gentleman who should have been suggested to the Civil Service Commission, whereas a promotion should have been made from the employees. Surely my hon. friend will admit that the head of the department has got certain rights in that respect, and that he certainly has the right to submit to the Civil Service Commission the name of a gentleman to be appointed as sub-head of his department. That surely goes without saying. The appointment has been made on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission; it has been regularly made.
You have not the proper certificate from the deputy head.
There was no deputy head.
Then you have no jurisdiction.
Does this mean that if you have no deputy head of the department, no appointment can be made?

No, because my hon.
friend knows that under the Civil Service Act he has a right to appoint a deputy minister. They did not appoint a deputy minister, they proceeded in an irregular man-91}
ner, without jurisdiction, and appointed a man, not deputy minister, but simply to draw $3,300 and be educated in order that he could be made deputy minister. That is what we find fault with. I know what the law is; I know my hon. friend could have appointed a man deputy minister, but the man was not fit to be appointed deputy minister and therefore they had to break and violate the law, and appoint him without a proper certificate. My hon. friend admits that they have no jurisdiction and he says:	Well, what are we going to do
about it? I say, do nothing, follow the law, and you will not get into these scrapes.
We have followed the law.

The committee are losing
sight of an important section of the Act:
If the deputy head reports that the knowledge and ability requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head of the department, based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination .. . provided the said person obtains from the commission a certificate, to be given with or without examination, as is determined by the regulations of the commission.
The first thing was to get a report from the deputy minister or the acting deputy minister. There is a reference to the report of the acting deputy minister in the report of the Civil Service Commission. There was a person acting in the place of a deputy head and if he had made a recommendation, the Governor in Council would have passed upon it. It appears to me that none of these conditions were complied with. The Postmaster General admits that there was no Teport from the deputy minister or deputy head of the department, and all he has read is a certificate from the Civil Service Commission that this person had all the necessary qualifications; but they only said so as an echo of the report given to them by the acting deputy head of the department. This deputy head should have reported that he had the ability requisite for the position and that it was wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar. There is no such report as that and that is the only report upon which the Civil Service Commission could intelligently act. I repeat that not one of the requirements necessary under section 21 has been complied with and there is the further fact that the Civil Service law was set in defiance by reason of the

applicant for the position not being obliged to undergo an examination. I think this is an extremely serious matter, and the explanation of the Postmaster General has not put it in any better light than it was in before he- contributed to the debate.

I must say I have
done my best. If I have not succeeded-
When the Postmaster General, with his ability, fails to make a better defence than he has done, it is evident that no defence is possible.

The minister says
that he wrote the Civil Service Commission requesting them to carry out the recommendation of the Government.
I did not say that.
They indicated that in his department the executive officers had made certain recommendations to this commission which they refused.
Yes.

What were those
recommendations?

I think I could name one, but I will bring them before the committee when my Estimates are up. There are in my department men, deserving men, not appointed by me, who were in the department when I assumed office, and whom I am told are deserving and ought to be kept in the department, men who every one, my deputy minister, and all the important officia's in the department, think should be promoted, and then Mr. Shortt says, no.
Do you think the Civil Service Commission are wrong?

I do, and I hope,
without betraying any secrets, that the law will be amended in such a way that the head and the deputy head-
Trust them for that.

My hon. friend may say what he likes, but if you have in your department a man who works well, who gives you satisfaction, who will work night and day when 'his services are required, and you feel that you ought to give 'him a chance to be promoted and you are told by a .man who does not know anything about the inside workings of the department that you must not promote that man, it is too bad.

Pretty hard. Then
what are you going to do with the Civil

Service reform which was one of the chief planks of the policy of this Government? I understood they were going to extend the beautiful policy of Civil Service reform to the outside service.

That is coming, my
dear friend.

My ihon. friend is
doing his best to smash up what we have.

My hon. friend is complaining while he has the remedy in his own hands, but has not chosen to apply it. At the last session provision was made for the appointment of a third member of the Civil Service Commission.
I know.

That appointment has not yet been made. If that appointment had been made the promotions to which my hon. friend refers could be made, even although the member of the commission whom he has indicated had objected.

I must say my hon. friend is absolutely right, and when a man is right, whether in opposition or not, it is proper to tell him so. If we have had these difficulties, it is probably because we have not appointed that third member of the commission; but these things will cure themselves by and by.

That is the end of the commission, then.
